rat_h1: Hotel prices by country – why they differ and how to book cheaper
rat_intro: Anyone who has booked a hotel may know the phenomenon: the same room, the same travel dates – and yet the booking site shows a different price depending on the country. In this guide we explain why that happens, what the legal position is, and how to compare fairly for your actual trip instead of trusting blanket promises.
rat_h2_warum: Why does the same room cost different amounts in different countries?
rat_warum_p1: Large booking platforms such as Booking.com present prices regionally. The amount shown depends, among other things, on which country the request comes from. Several factors are behind this: differing purchasing power and price levels in the target markets, exchange rates and the currency displayed, local demand and competition, and country-specific marketing campaigns and discounts. The way taxes and fees are shown also differs: in some countries the price appears inclusive of all charges, in others taxes are added separately.
rat_warum_p2: The result: for one and the same stay, noticeably different prices can arise depending on "which country you are looking from". A comparison is therefore only meaningful if all amounts are set side by side including taxes and fees and in the same currency.
rat_h2_erlaubt: Is it allowed to compare and book this way?
rat_erlaubt_p: Comparing publicly visible prices is completely normal and everyday – price comparison sites do nothing else. Actually booking from another country, for example through a VPN, is a legal grey area and depends on the particular terms of the booking platform. Within the EU there is the so-called Geo-blocking Regulation, which is intended to limit discrimination against customers based on where they live; how it applies in an individual case is complex, however. This guide is not legal advice – using a VPN is at your own responsibility and subject to the applicable terms of the platform and the VPN provider.
rat_h2_pruefen: How to check whether your stay is cheaper elsewhere
rat_pruefen_p: That is exactly what GeoRates is for. You simply paste the link to the hotel you want on Booking.com, choose the room, the board type and the cancellation condition – and we automatically retrieve the publicly displayed price for that room through sessions from several countries. All prices are converted including taxes and at the current exchange rate into euros, so you can see at a glance whether the same stay is cheaper when viewed from another country. To the free price check →
rat_h2_vpn: VPN – what to watch out for
rat_vpn_p: If a lower price turns up via another country, in practice it can often only be obtained with a VPN from that country. Keep a few points in mind: check the payment currency and any foreign currency fees on your card, check the cancellation conditions, and make sure it really is the same room and the same dates. A card with favourable currency conversion can avoid additional conversion costs. The note about using a VPN is purely informational.
rat_h2_tipps: Practical tips for a fair price comparison
rat_tipp1: Always compare including taxes and fees – otherwise a price looks cheaper than it turns out to be.
rat_tipp2: Make sure the room category and board type are identical (for example breakfast included versus for a surcharge).
rat_tipp3: Check the cancellation conditions: "free cancellation" is often somewhat more expensive than "non-refundable".
rat_tipp4: Keep an eye on the payment currency and the exchange rate.
rat_tipp5: To be safe, take a screenshot of the offer you intend to book.
rat_faq1_q: Are hotels really cheaper from another country?
rat_faq1_a: Sometimes yes, often not. Whether a difference arises depends on the hotel, the travel dates and the platform – which is why it is worth comparing for your particular case.
rat_faq2_q: Do I need a VPN in order to compare?
rat_faq2_a: No. For comparing, GeoRates retrieves the publicly displayed prices from several countries for you. You only need a VPN if you want to book from another country yourself.
rat_faq3_a: Yes. The automatic price check is free and can be used without signing up.
rat_faq4_a: No. GeoRates is an independent comparison tool and has no partnership with Booking.com. You make the booking yourself, directly on the platform.

lp_title: Booking.com prices by country: how often do they pay off? | GeoRates
lp_h1: Booking.com country prices: what they are and how often they are worth it
lp_intro: Booking.com can show the same room, on the same dates, at a different price depending on the country. That is not a myth, and it is not a trick that always works. Here is how country prices come about, and what our measurements actually show.
lp_woher_p: Hotels can set so-called prices for specific countries on Booking.com: a discount of at least 5% that only guests see when they use the platform from certain countries or regions (Booking.com for Partners). Booking says these discounts can be combined with Genius, early-booker and last-minute offers, but not with mobile rates or time-limited deals.
lp_woher_p2: Other effects look like country prices and are not: exchange rates, rounded conversions, taxes that are included one time and not the next, and Genius discounts that appear in some sessions and not in others.
lp_h2_eu: Why a VPN inside the EU usually does nothing
lp_eu_p: The EU Geo-blocking Regulation forbids offering customers in the EU different prices or conditions because of nationality or place of residence. That expressly includes hotels (Verbraucherzentrale, EUR-Lex). Switching from Germany to Spain therefore usually brings no price advantage. Countries outside the EEA are the interesting ones.

jp_intro: Japan does not stand out in our log because it wins most often. The USA was the cheapest country 42 times by at least 1%, India 30 times, Japan 22 times. When Japan does win, the saving is higher on average than for those more frequent countries: 12.8% on average, 11.0% median, one case of 38.1%. Argentina’s average is higher at 17.7%, but on only 5 hits. Japan is not a country to switch to blindly. It is one worth checking when the stay is expensive.
jp_daten_p: The log covers 223 checks with a result from 16 Sep to 4 Nov 2026, almost all starting from Germany, across 139 hotels. GeoRates requests the same room, the same board, the same cancellation terms and the same dates from 15 country sessions in the same run, including taxes and fees, in euros. We do not count a gap below 1% as a find.
jp_li1: On hits of 1% or more, Japan was the cheapest country 22 times. Across all 223 checks Japan was listed as the best country 40 times. The difference is cases below 1%, mostly rounding and not a real lead.
jp_li2: On those 22 hits the saving averaged 12.8%, with a median of 11.0% and a maximum of 38.1%. 12.8% is the average of those hits, not of every check. Across all checks with a result the median was 2.2%.
jp_li3: More often, but lower on average: the USA 42 hits at 6.7%, India 30 at 8.4%, Colombia 19 at 6.0% (median there only 1.5%). Forums often call Colombia a bargain country; in this log the typical hit is small.
jp_li4: Argentina averaged 17.7% across 5 hits, including an outlier of 51.1% (€400.01 → €195.58, a hotel in Thailand, 20 Sep 2026). Peru averaged 11.7% across 4 hits, below Japan.
jp_li5: A concrete find on 20 Sep 2026, after the method correction: €267 at the start, €165.22 via Japan. That is €101.78 and the 38.1% recorded in the log. It is the highest Japan figure in the log, not the typical one.
jp_zeitraum: On 18 Sep 2026 the measurement gained a Genius correction. Before that (83 result rows, 16–18 Sep) the share with at least 1% saving was 55.4%, the average 5.61% and the median 3.3%. From 19 Sep (140 rows) the figures were 62.1%, average 4.46%, median 2.1%. That is for all countries together. In the narrower window from 19 Sep (140 checks) Japan was the cheapest country by at least 1% only 6 times, average 12.0%, median 8.5%, maximum still 38.1%. The 22 hits and the 12.8% on this page refer to the whole log from 16 Sep, including the days before the correction. The narrower table is in the country ranking. 19 rows later carry a Genius flag; earlier rows cannot be checked that way.
jp_fazit: In short: when Japan wins in this log, the gap is larger on average than for the USA, India or Colombia. Whether that is true for your hotel only a check of that exact room can say. The largest euro saving in the log was not via Japan but via India: €553.54 on 17 Sep 2026, before the correction (€2,873.40 → €2,319.86).
jp_warum_p: We do not know for certain. A plausible explanation is that hotels can set discounts for specific countries and regions on Booking.com (Booking.com for Partners). We only measure what the session displays. Exchange rates, rounded conversions and discounts that appear in only some sessions can also look like a country price.
jp_haken1: Savings are not always stable. In the whole log 15 rows are marked “not stable” and 33 “stable”. The mark is not broken down by country, so not for Japan either. We cannot say how many of the 22 Japan hits would have survived a second fetch.
jp_haken2: 22 hits are a small sample. The median of 11.0% sits close to the average of 12.8%; the single 38.1% case still pulls the average up. Neither figure is a promise for the next booking.
jp_haken3: Inside the EU, switching country usually does nothing because of the Geo-blocking Regulation (Verbraucherzentrale, EUR-Lex). Japan is outside the EEA, so a Japan session is not covered by that rule. Switching from Germany to Spain stays uninteresting.

jp_s3: Check the room, the board, the cancellation terms and the final price including taxes. A non-refundable rate is not a fair comparison with a flexible one.

jp_s5: If the rate says “residents of Japan only”, do not book it.

tr_title: Booking from Turkey on Booking.com: is it worth it? | GeoRates
tr_meta_desc: Turkey is a common VPN tip for cheaper Booking.com rates. We do not measure from Turkey, and we say so plainly: hotels in Turkey were lately about 4% cheaper from India.
tr_h1: Booking from Turkey on Booking.com: what we know and what we don’t
tr_intro: Turkey shows up in plenty of VPN guides as a country where hotels are supposed to be cheaper. Before you go looking for a Turkish VPN server, here is an honest frame: Turkey is not one of the 15 countries GeoRates measures from. We therefore cannot say with any confidence whether Booking.com is cheaper from Turkey. What we can show is how prices for hotels in Turkey behaved in our measurements.
tr_h2_daten: What our data shows (and what it doesn’t)
tr_li1: GeoRates compares the same room, in the same run, from 15 country sessions: Germany, Colombia, Argentina, Egypt, India, Vietnam, Indonesia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Peru, Mexico, the Philippines, Thailand, the United States and Japan. Turkey is not among them.
tr_li2: On two checks for hotels in Turkey, GeoRates also tried a Turkish session. Both times Turkey returned no price. There is therefore no measured “Turkey price” in our log.
tr_li3: For hotels in Turkey, the GeoRates log (16 Sep–7 Nov 2026) has 10 checks with a result, covering 5 hotels. Only 2 of them are from after our Genius correction on 18 Sep.
tr_neu1: All-inclusive resort, double room, not free to cancel (21 Sep 2026): €968.09 from Germany, €929.67 from India, so €38.42 (4.0%) less. Japan was almost level, at 3.8% less, and Argentina was 7.5% more expensive. This check was not fetched a second time.
tr_neu2: All-inclusive suite (5 Nov 2026, baseline country Australia): €3,470.01 against €3,343.29 from India, so €126.72 (3.7%) less. A second fetch confirmed the figure. From Thailand, the United States and Japan the same suite was about 7.7% more expensive than from Germany.
tr_frueher: Earlier measurements (16–18 Sep 2026, before the Genius correction, only partly informative): hotels in Istanbul, at Istanbul airport and in Antalya-Konyaaltı. Depending on the room, India, Japan, the United States or Indonesia came out ahead, by 0.3% to 13.3%. At one Istanbul hotel the cheapest country changed from room to room.
tr_fazit: The sample is small. It does show that hotels in Turkey can have country prices, and that India was ahead in both of our more recent cases. Whether it would be cheaper still from Turkey itself, we do not know.
tr_h2_warum: Why country prices are possible for hotels in Turkey
tr_warum_p: Hotels can set discounts on Booking.com for particular countries or regions (Booking.com for Partners). Turkey is not in the EU. The EU Geo-blocking Regulation, which forbids price differences by place of residence inside the EU (Verbraucherzentrale), does not apply to prices shown to visitors from Turkey. Country prices are therefore possible in principle. How often, and how large, we cannot say without our own Turkey measurement.
tr_haken1: No Turkey data of our own: claims such as “always X% cheaper from Turkey” we can neither confirm nor refute.
tr_haken2: Check that the terms match: all-inclusive, room category and cancellation terms have to be identical. Otherwise you are comparing different offers.
tr_haken3: Resident-only rates: if a rate says it is only for residents or nationals of a country, you should not book it. That can cause trouble at check-in.
tr_haken4: Paying in lira: if you pay in Turkish lira (TRY), use a card with no foreign-currency fee and decline Booking’s conversion into euros.
tr_s1: Check your hotel with GeoRates first. In one run you see whether one of the 15 measured countries (India, for example) is cheaper.
tr_s2: If you also want to test Turkey, connect a VPN to a Turkish server and open Booking.com in a private window.
tr_s3: Compare exactly the same room, with the same board and the same cancellation terms, and always the final price including taxes and fees.
tr_s4: Book the country with the lowest final price, and pay in local currency with a card that has no foreign-currency fee.

eg_title: Is Booking.com cheaper from Egypt? Why 0.2% is not a saving | GeoRates
eg_meta_desc: Egypt often shows up as the cheapest country in price comparisons, usually by only a few cents. Our measurements show when Egypt really was cheaper, and why that is rare.
eg_h1: Is Egypt the cheapest? Why 0.2% is not a saving
eg_intro: If you compare Booking.com prices across several countries, Egypt turns up surprisingly often as the “cheapest country”. It sounds like a saving tip. In our data it usually isn’t one: Egypt almost always wins by only a few cents.
eg_daten_lead: From the GeoRates log (16 Sep–7 Nov 2026, all prices including taxes and fees, converted into euros):
eg_li1: Egypt was the cheapest country 22 times. In 17 of those cases the advantage was only 0.1% to 0.4%, which is €0.13 to €2.46, median €0.50.
eg_li2: Egypt was at least 1% cheaper only 4 times (3.6%, 5.9%, 6.5% and 9.8%). The two cases after our Genius correction on 18 Sep (9.8% and 5.9%) were not stable on the second fetch.
eg_li3: Since 19 Sep we have had the Egypt price right next to the German price for 120 checks. Result: in 88 cases (73%) Egypt was within ±1% of the German price, in 20 cases it was at least 1% more expensive, and in 12 cases at least 1% cheaper. Median difference: 0.03%.
eg_li4: In 11 of those 12 cases another country was cheaper still than Egypt, for example Peru, India or Argentina.
eg_beispiel: A typical example from the log: a hotel in Munich cost €164 from Germany and 9,837 EGP from Egypt, which converts to €163.77. GeoRates showed Egypt as the cheapest country, with a difference of €0.23. That is not a saving. It is rounding.
eg_warum_p1: The likely reason is the conversion. Booking.com shows the price in Egyptian pounds, rounded to a whole amount. Convert that back into euros and the figure sometimes lands a few cents under the German price. With 15 countries compared, it is almost certain that one of them leads by a few cents because of rounding. Peru had the same effect in our data.
eg_warum_p2: That is why GeoRates treats differences under 1% as “no difference”.
eg_wann_p1: When Egypt was clearly cheaper, another country was usually clearly cheaper as well. A plausible explanation: the hotel set a discount for several countries or regions outside the EU (Booking.com for Partners). We do not know that for certain. We only measure what is displayed. For you that means checking Egypt alone is not enough.
eg_wann_p2: Egypt is outside the EU. The EU Geo-blocking Regulation, which forbids price differences by place of residence inside the EU (Verbraucherzentrale), therefore does not apply to Egyptian prices. Country prices are possible, but they rarely show up in our data.
eg_haken1: Conversion costs eat tiny savings: if you pay in Egyptian pounds (EGP), you risk a foreign-currency or conversion fee. With an advantage of a few cents you are almost certainly more expensive in the end.
eg_haken2: Unstable hits: both of the larger Egypt savings since 19 Sep came out smaller on the second fetch and were marked not stable.
eg_haken3: More effort, no gain: a VPN, a private window and a new search, just to save a few cents, is not worth it.
eg_s1: Check your hotel with GeoRates. All 15 countries are compared in the same run.
eg_s2: Ignore differences under 1%. That is usually rounding.
eg_s3: If Egypt is clearly cheaper, look whether another country is cheaper still.
eg_s4: Factor in fees: if you pay in a foreign currency you need a card with no foreign-currency fee, or the saving disappears quickly.

eu_title: Is a VPN worth it for hotels inside the EU? Geo-blocking explained | GeoRates
eu_meta_desc: Book Spain, Italy or Greece cheaper through a VPN? Our measurements show that EU countries almost always returned the same price as Germany. Why that is, and which countries are worth a look instead.
eu_h1: Is a VPN worth it inside the EU? The Geo-blocking Regulation explained
eu_intro: A popular tip goes: “Just book your hotel in Spain through a Spanish VPN server and it will be cheaper.” That sounds logical, but inside the EU it usually does not work. Here is why, and what our measurements show.
eu_regel_p1: The EU Geo-blocking Regulation forbids traders from offering customers in the EU different prices or conditions because of their nationality, place of residence or location. That expressly includes hotel stays (Verbraucherzentrale, EUR-Lex). A hotel in Mallorca may not, as a rule, charge you more from Germany than it charges someone from Spain.
eu_regel_p2: That does not apply to countries outside the EU. Hotels can set discounts on Booking.com for particular countries or regions (Booking.com for Partners), for example for guests from the United States or India.
eu_daten_lead: Alongside the 15 fixed countries (all of them outside the EU except Germany), GeoRates sometimes also asks for the country the hotel is in. Since 19 Sep 2026 that has given us prices from EU countries such as Spain, Italy, Portugal, Greece and Croatia in 37 checks, 42 EU prices in all.
eu_li1: 33 of 42 EU prices were within ±1% of the German price, and most of them matched to the cent.
eu_li2: 3 were cheaper, 6 were more expensive. In 5 of those 9 gaps the same price also appeared in one of the German control fetches. The price was already moving inside Germany.
eu_li3: For comparison: in 26 of 87 checks with several German fetches, the German price itself already moved by at least 1%.
eu_li4: It was similar for users in Austria and France: in 6 of 8 cases their home-country price matched the German one, and the 2 gaps also showed up in German fetches.
eu_contrast: In those same 37 checks, a country outside the EU was at least 1% cheaper 21 times, and 10% or more 8 times. Most often: the United States (12), India (6), Colombia (2), Peru (1).
eu_hotels: Across all hotels in EU countries since 19 Sep (47 checks with a result), another country was at least 1% cheaper in 28 cases, almost always the United States (21) or India (6). The median of those hits: 4.65%.
eu_fazit: A Spanish or Italian VPN server does next to nothing in our data. Countries outside the EU are the interesting ones, including for hotels in Europe.
eu_haken1: A moving price is not a country price: search twice in a row and you sometimes see different prices, even without a VPN. Compare only checks from the same run.
eu_haken2: Genius and mobile rates: these discounts are tied to your account or device, not to the country, and they distort the comparison.
eu_haken3: Switzerland and the United Kingdom are not in the EU. We have little or no measurement data for them, so we make no claim here.
eu_haken4: Actually getting a non-EU price: if you pay in a foreign currency, you need a card with no foreign-currency fee. Do not book “residents only” rates.
eu_s1: Skip trying EU servers one by one.
eu_s2: Check your hotel with GeoRates. It compares 14 countries outside the EU with the German price, in the same run and including taxes.
eu_s3: If a non-EU country is at least a few percent cheaper, connect a VPN to that country and book there.
eu_s4: Check the room, board, cancellation terms and final price before you pay.

eu_faq1_q: Does a VPN with an EU server produce cheaper hotel prices?
eu_faq1_a: Almost never in our data. 33 of 42 EU prices were within ±1% of the German price, and the gaps were mostly explained by ordinary price movement.
eu_faq2_q: Why are prices the same inside the EU?
eu_faq2_a: The EU Geo-blocking Regulation forbids different prices or conditions by nationality or place of residence inside the EU, including for hotels.
eu_faq3_q: Can a hotel in Spain be cheaper from the United States?
eu_faq3_a: Yes. The regulation applies only inside the EU. In our data, hotels in EU countries were cheapest most often from the United States.
eu_faq4_q: Which countries are worth it instead?
eu_faq4_a: In our data, mainly the United States and India. It depends on the hotel, though, so the check is worth doing for each booking.
eu_faq5_q: Is booking with a VPN legal?
eu_faq5_a: Using a VPN is legal in Germany. You should not book rates that are expressly only for residents.
